blocks.heading: Graphs
blocks.text: A graph describes relationships between objects. Its points are vertices or nodes; its connections are edges. We write G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set and E is the edge set. These graphs differ from charts used to display numerical data.

blocks.heading: Origins and example
blocks.text:
Graph theory grew from Euler’s study of the bridges of Königsberg.

For V = {a, b, c, d} and E = {ab, ac, bd, cd}, the graph has four vertices and four edges. Edge ab connects a and b.

blocks.heading: Directed graphs
blocks.text: A directed graph assigns a direction to each edge. An arrow A → B permits travel from A to B; it does not imply an arrow B → A. Example: A → B, B → C, and C → A form a directed cycle.

blocks.heading: Undirected graphs
blocks.text: An undirected graph has edges without arrows. An edge between A and B connects them in both directions. A drawing’s edge length or shape does not change which vertices it connects.

blocks.heading: Degree
blocks.text: The degree of a vertex is its number of incident edges. In an undirected graph, a loop contributes 2 to degree. If vertex 30 connects to two neighbors, deg(30) = 2. If vertex 60 has three incident non-loop edges, deg(60) = 3.

blocks.heading: Paths
blocks.text: A path is a sequence of adjacent vertices with no repeated vertex. Consecutive vertices must be joined by an edge. In a directed graph, follow the arrow direction. Example: 6 → 8 → 3 → 1 → 2 → 4, provided those edges exist.

blocks.heading: Cycles
blocks.text: A simple cycle returns to its starting vertex without repeating any other vertex or edge. Example: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 1, when all the required edges exist. The cycle graph Cn consists of a single cycle through n vertices, for n ≥ 3.
